primitives.summary:
AuthScreen — a whole sign-in screen: branding, social providers, the
email form with a "Forgot password?" link, and a footer (terms, a
sign-up link). It assembles the auth primitives (`AuthBranding`,
`SocialAuthRow`, `AuthForm`, `ForgotPasswordLink`) so an app passes
props instead of composing them.

The form stays above the keyboard on small phones: with the app's
`KeyboardScrollProvider` (react-native-keyboard-controller), else with
`KeyboardAvoidingView`. With the provider's `toolbar` (`KeyboardToolbar`),
a previous / next / done bar rides above the keyboard. In development, on
iOS, it warns when a third-party provider is offered without Sign in with
Apple (App Store Review Guideline 4.8 rejects that). `appleProvider()`
adds Apple's own button in one line.

`slotProps` feeds a default part. Composing the primitives yourself is
still the escape hatch.

FullScreenModal — content that takes the whole screen over the app: a
photo or video viewer, a camera, a scanner.

(`overFullScreen` on iOS; under the system bars on Android), faded in (no
animation with Reduce Motion). `tone="dark"` (the default) is a black
backdrop with light status bar content, for media; `tone="app"` is the
theme's background; `tone="none"` draws no backdrop, for content that
draws its own (a viewer that fades to show the app as it's dragged away,
with `FULL_SCREEN_DARK` behind it). Content
gets its own safe area (`useSafeAreaInsets` inside is the modal's) and
places its own close control: Android back and the VoiceOver escape
gesture call `onOpenChange(false)`.

<NativeDialog>.

primitives.summary:
InboxPage — a list of conversations or tickets: unread state, a time, a
preview line, swipe actions, pull to refresh, paging and an empty state.

Generic: the rows are whatever the app has (support reports, direct
messages, an idea board). Data and actions come in as props; the layout
draws them the platform's way. On iOS it is the Settings app's inset
grouped style, like `SettingsPage`: the page is `groupedBackground`, the
rows one rounded group on `surface` with hairline separators that start at
the text. On Android rows are full width.

Swipe actions: each row's `swipeActions` are always reachable without a
gesture library, as VoiceOver / TalkBack custom actions and on long press
(a menu). For the swipe itself, fill the `swipeable` slot with your
gesture-handler wrapper (`ReanimatedSwipeable` from
react-native-gesture-handler, an optional peer); it receives the actions
and the row.

Rows: `avatar` puts a picture of who it is between the unread dot and the
text (an unread count shows at the end of the row, as in Mail); `leading`
replaces the dot.

Slots: `row`, `swipeable`, `header` (above the group), `footer` (below it,
the paging spinner by default) and `empty`. `slots` swaps a part for your
component (same props), `slotProps` feeds the default more props, `null`
drops it.

Composes `<ScreenContainer scroll>` underneath, renders a sectioned
`ListItem` list, and surfaces an optional dangerous-action footer
(e.g., "Sign out", "Delete account") in destructive tone.

Why ship a layout: every consumer rebuilds this list with the same
three pieces (sections → rows → footer). Genesis ships the assembly so
consumers compose, not rebuild.

Layer-3 customization: pass `headerTitle`, `headerLeft`, `headerRight`,
`large`, `scrollEdgeBehavior`, OR a direct `headerOptions={...}`
passthrough. The composed options are rendered via the consumer's own
`<Stack.Screen options={...}>` — see `getStackScreenOptions()` helper.

app's inset grouped style: the page is `systemGroupedBackground`, each
section a rounded group of cells on `secondarySystemGroupedBackground` with
hairline `separator` lines between cells, inset from the leading edge to
the cell text; the header is an uppercase footnote in `secondaryLabel`
above the group and the footnote sits under it in the same color. On
Android, cells are full width and the header is a Material subheader in the
theme's primary color. Neither platform draws a band or a rule behind a
header. Cell content itself is `NativeListItem`'s.

swaps a part (`sectionHeader`, `row`, `footnote`, `dangerousActions`) for
your component, which receives exactly the props the default would;
`slotProps` feeds the default more props; `null` drops the part.

doesn't fit.

Sheet / BottomSheet — modal that slides up from the bottom.

Use for non-blocking selections, filters, and short flows that benefit
from preserving screen context. For blocking confirmations, use
<NativeDialog>. For full-screen flows, use a navigation route.

By default this is React Native's own `Modal`, which needs nothing mounted
above it: the system page sheet on iOS (swipe down to close) and a bottom
panel over a scrim on Android (back button or a tap on the scrim closes
it). Content gets its own safe area (`useSafeAreaInsets` inside the sheet
is the sheet's), and the bottom inset is padded. Put scrolling content in
`NativeSheetScrollView`. The sheet doesn't move above the keyboard.

`@gorhom/bottom-sheet` (snap points, drag between heights) is used only
when the app opts in by mounting `<NativeSheetProvider bottomSheet={…}>`
(or passing `bottomSheet` to `GenesisNativeApp`), never because the
library happens to be installed: it throws on open unless its
`BottomSheetModalProvider` is mounted, and it needs gesture-handler's
`GestureHandlerRootView` at the root and Reanimated set up.
`snapPoints` and `initialSnapIndex` apply only to that path.

A short menu or form passes `fitContent`: the sheet is as tall as what is in it.

A sheet that is a screen of its own (a link can open it) belongs in the
router instead: an expo-router screen with `presentation: "formSheet"` and
`sheetAllowedDetents` (e.g. `[0.5, 1]`) is the system sheet with detents.

The pattern for every icon-only control: hide the glyph from assistive tech
and put a real, visually-hidden string next to it. Done by hand this is
three easily-forgotten steps (`aria-hidden` on the SVG, `focusable="false"`
for IE/Edge-era SVG focus behavior, a `VisuallyHidden` sibling), and getting
one wrong produces a control announced as "button" with no name — which
looks completely fine on screen.

and appends the hidden label, so there is no DOM node to attach a `ref` or a
`className` to and, deliberately, no `forwardRef` here — unlike every other
primitive in this folder. Style the icon or the surrounding control instead.

    <TrashIcon />
  </AccessibleIcon>
</Button>

BuilderLayout — the three columns of a builder: an outline of the parts on
the left, the editor for the selected part in the centre, a live preview
on the right.

```tsx
<BuilderLayout
  outline={<QuestionList />}
  outlineLabel="Outline"
  editor={<QuestionEditor key={selectedId} />}
  preview={<LivePreview />}
  previewLabel="Preview"
  sticky
/>
```

Responsive by container query, so it needs no knowledge of the page around
it: all three columns from a 56rem container, wider side columns from
76rem, the preview under the editor below 56rem and everything stacked
below 34rem (see `GRID` for each slot combination). The preview keeps its
place in the tree when the editor or outline changes, so it never
remounts; changing `previewLabel` between set and unset does remount it
(the element changes from `<div>` to `<aside>`).

It positions the three parts and nothing else. It does **not** own tabs,
the app rail or a page header: those belong to the shell. Put a builder's
sections in `useAppShellSubNav` (or your own tabs inside `editor`) and its
title, status and actions in `AppShellPageHeader`. To keep one preview
across sections, render one `BuilderLayout` around the sections and swap
`editor`; nest a second one (outline and editor only) inside a section
that has an outline.

primitives.summary:
DashboardPage — a stat row over a flexible region of charts, tables and
sections.

```tsx
<DashboardPage
  title="This quarter"
  subtitle="1 Apr – 30 Jun"
  actions={<DatePicker … />}
  stats={
    <>
      <StatCard label="Active clients" value={42} />
      <StatCard label="Sessions" value={318} trend={{ value: 12, label: "vs Q1" }} />
    </>
  }
>
  <Section title="Revenue"><ChartContainer …/></Section>
  <Section title="At risk"><DataTable …/></Section>
</DashboardPage>
```

The two regions are separated on purpose. Stats are a fixed-shape row that
must reflow as a unit; everything below is free-form and stacks. Folding
both into one `children` is how the stat row ends up hand-gridded per page,
with a different breakpoint each time — the exact drift `Grid` exists to
stop.

Children stack at `gap-8`, wider than the page's own `gap-6`, so a chart
and the table under it don't read as one block.

The header row is markup, not a component, and deliberately not
`PageHeader` — see `./detail-page` for the measured reasons composing it
was rejected across all four templates. Width is left to `Container` —
wrap, don't duplicate.

This is a **layout**: it positions tiles and regions and never fetches a
metric. There is deliberately no data-bound twin — binding a dashboard
needs an aggregate/metric contract, and `genesis-core` ships none. Adding
a template ahead of its contract is what `docs/FRAMEWORK.md` warns against
in "Why templates need the contract first".

primitives.summary:
DetailPage — one record's full view: a title row with actions, a primary
content region, and a metadata sidebar that drops below the content on
small screens.

```tsx
<DetailPage
  breadcrumb={<Breadcrumb>…</Breadcrumb>}
  title={person.name}
  subtitle={person.role}
  actions={<Button testID="edit">Edit</Button>}
  sidebar={
    <Stack gap="lg">
      <StatCard label="Sessions" value={12} />
      <SettingsRow label="Owner">{person.owner}</SettingsRow>
    </Stack>
  }
>
  <Section title="Timeline">{…}</Section>
</DetailPage>
```

`Split` is the backbone, at `ratio="2/3"` — content takes eight of twelve
tracks, metadata four. Reading order is content-then-metadata in the DOM,
which is also the order they stack in, so a phone shows the record before
its provenance rather than after it.

This is a **layout**: it positions three regions and never asks what is in
them. Fetching the record is the caller's job — or
`ResourceDetailPage` from `@marktiderman/genesis-ui/data`, which is this
component with `useOne` wired to its title, content and sidebar.

The header row is markup, not a component, and deliberately not
`PageHeader` — which now sits in this same folder, so composing it would
be legal. It was tried and measured, and it does not fit:

1. `PageHeader.title` and `.subtitle` are `string`. Every template's title
   would narrow from `ReactNode`, and a record heading is the one place a
   `StatusBadge` beside the name is routine.
2. `@marktiderman/genesis-ui/detail-page`'s emitted closure goes from
   5.8 KB / 5 chunks to 34.4 KB / 14, and picks up a runtime dependency on
   `radix-ui` (Popover, Collapsible, Switch, and Select via `ViewSettings`)
   — for a header that renders a title, a line under it and a slot, and
   mounts none of that. Per-component subpaths exist so a consumer does
   not pay for what they did not import.
3. `PageHeader` has no slot above the title, and hard-codes
   `data-testid="page-title"` on its `<h1>`.

Not a reason, having checked it: RSC. `PageHeader` is `"use client"`, but
the emitted `detail-page.js` is NOT stamped with the directive when it
imports it — a server module importing a client module is the ordinary
boundary. What would make folding correct is upstream: widen `title` /
`subtitle` to `ReactNode`, and lift the list chrome out of `PageHeader`.

Width is deliberately not an opinion here. `Container` already answers
"how wide is this page", so wrap rather than duplicate:
`<Container size="lg"><DetailPage … /></Container>`. Under `AppShell`,
whose `<main>` already pads, most pages want neither.

primitives.summary:
FormPage — a titled form: header, validation summary, a body of sections,
and a sticky action bar.

It renders a real `<form>` and forwards `onSubmit` (and every other form
attribute), so a plain `type="submit"` button in `actions` submits it with
no `form=` wiring. That is what keeps it usable for a HAND-WRITTEN form —
`react-hook-form`, `useActionState`, or an uncontrolled `<form action>` —
rather than only for one of them.

**Do not put a `ResourceForm` inside it.** `ResourceForm` renders its own
`<form>`, and nesting one form in another is invalid HTML: the browser
drops the inner element, SSR and hydration disagree about the tree, and a
submit fires both handlers. `ResourceForm` is the data-bound *alternative*
to this template — it already answers "bind a form to a resource", with a
`layout="page"` mode of its own — not something this one wraps.

```tsx
<FormPage
  title="New engagement"
  description="Both parties will be notified."
  errors={submitFailed ? "Fix the highlighted fields." : undefined}
  onSubmit={handleSubmit(onValid)}
  actions={
    <>
      <Button variant="ghost" type="button" testID="cancel">Cancel</Button>
      <Button type="submit" testID="save">Save</Button>
    </>
  }
>
  <Section title="Basics">
    <FormField label="Name">…</FormField>
  </Section>
</FormPage>
```

Sections are just children — `Section` is the natural one, but any node
works. The body spaces them at `gap-8`, wider than the page's own `gap-6`,
so section boundaries read as boundaries rather than as more fields.

The sticky bar needs a scrolling ancestor to stick to, which `AppShell`'s
`<main>` provides. It renders only when `actions` is set: an empty sticky
strip is a border floating over the content for no reason.

This is a **layout** — it positions a form, it does not submit one. Binding
fields to a resource is `ResourceForm`'s job
(`@marktiderman/genesis-ui/data`), which is already the one home for that
question. The header row is markup, not a component, and deliberately not
`PageHeader` — see `./detail-page` for the measured reasons composing it
was rejected across all four templates (`title: string`, and a 6x jump in
the emitted per-component closure plus a new `radix-ui` runtime dependency
for chrome none of them render). Width is left to `Container` for the
one-home reason — wrap, don't duplicate.

primitives.summary:
Grid — two-dimensional flow for card and tile collections.

`cols` is the count at the widest breakpoint; the class it emits is a
responsive ramp, so a card grid reflows on its own without the consumer
writing a single breakpoint.

```tsx
<Grid cols={3} gap="lg">
  {people.map((p) => <PersonCard key={p.id} person={p} />)}
</Grid>

<Grid cols={4} gap="sm" align="start">
  {stats.map((s) => <StatCard key={s.id} {...s} />)}
</Grid>
```

Deliberately NOT here: `grid-template-areas`, explicit row/column
placement, and per-child spans. A component that positions a *named*
child has stopped positioning things without knowing what they are, and
a grid whose children each carry placement props is a CSS file wearing a
React costume — reach for `className` at that point.

components.name: isPathActive
components.summary:
Default active-path matcher, mirroring React Router's `NavLink` (prefix
match, with `/` treated as exact). Consumers can override via an `isActive`
prop where components accept one.

`activePath` may carry a query and hash (`pathname + search + hash`). An
item whose `to` has neither compares against the path part only, exactly as
before. An item that opts in by putting a query or hash in its `to`
(`/admin?tab=users`, `/settings#profile`) is active only when the path
matches exactly AND every query param it names has the same value in
`activePath` (extra params such as `&page=2` are ignored) AND, if it names a
hash, the hash is equal.

components.name: resolveNavigation
components.summary:
Resolve where `pathname` sits in a logical navigation tree. Pure: it never
reads browser history or `window`.

A node matches when its pattern matches a leading run of WHOLE path
segments (`/my` matches `/my/tasks`, never `/my-other`). Among matches the
winner is decided by positional specificity: at the first position where
one pattern is static and the other a `$param`, the static one wins (so
`/clients/new` beats `/clients/$clientId` whatever the sibling order, and
`/my` beats `/$space/tasks` for `/my/tasks`). Otherwise the pattern matching
more segments wins, then the deeper tree node.
Non-matching nodes are still searched, so a match keeps its logical
ancestors even when their URLs differ.

components.name: NavigationNode

segments are either static (`clients`) or named params (`$clientId`). A
node's place in the tree is its LOGICAL parent, which need not share its URL
prefix — `/clients/$clientId` can sit under `/dashboard`.

components.name: ResolvedNavigation

Result of {@link resolveNavigation}. `current`, `parent` and every `trail`
entry are shallow copies of their tree nodes with `path` interpolated from
`params` (a param the URL did not supply stays as `$name`).

primitives.summary:
PasswordToggleField — a password input with a show/hide control that keeps
focus and caret position across the toggle.

Composition:

```tsx
<PasswordToggleField>
  <PasswordToggleFieldInput placeholder="Password" />
  <PasswordToggleFieldToggle>
    <PasswordToggleFieldSlot visible={<EyeOff />} hidden={<Eye />} />
  </PasswordToggleFieldToggle>
</PasswordToggleField>
```

Why Radix and not five lines of `useState` plus `type={shown ? "text" :
"password"}`: the naive version loses the caret on every toggle, leaves the
button unlabelled (or labelled with a state that never updates), and — the
part nobody writes — leaves the password visible in the DOM after the form is
submitted or reset. Radix resets visibility on both `submit` and `reset`,
restores `selectionStart`/`selectionEnd` after the type swap, and derives the
toggle's `aria-label` ("Show password" / "Hide password") from the current
state unless the caller supplies text or a label of their own.

Radix's own root is a **context provider with no DOM node of its own**, so
this wrapper renders a `relative` box around the children. That box is
load-bearing, not decoration: `PasswordToggleFieldToggle` is positioned
`absolute`, and absolute positioning resolves against the nearest positioned
ancestor. Without a wrapper the toggle would escape the field and land
against whatever positioned ancestor the consumer's page happened to have —
or the initial containing block, i.e. the page corner. The composition
documented above would put the show/hide button nowhere near the input.

---

**Stability.** Radix ships this primitive as `unstable_PasswordToggleField`
and documents its API as subject to change; the underlying
`@radix-ui/react-password-toggle-field` package is still on `0.1.x`. It is
exported here under its stable-looking name for ergonomics, but it is the one
component in this package whose props may change in a minor release. Pin the
package if that is unacceptable, or compose `Input` + `Button` yourself.

primitives.summary:
ResourceDetailPage — `DetailPage` with a record bound to it: fetches one
record by id through the mounted `DataProvider` and hands it to the title,
the actions, the sidebar and the content.

```tsx
<ResourceDetailPage
  resource="people"
  id={params.id}
  subtitleField="role"
  actions={(person) => <Button testID="edit">Edit {person.name}</Button>}
  sidebar={(person) => <StatCard label="Sessions" value={person.session_count} />}
>
  {(person) => <Section title="Timeline"><Timeline personId={person.id} /></Section>}
</ResourceDetailPage>
```

This is the detail-route counterpart to `ResourcePage`, which is the list
one. Both are **data-bound**, not layouts: they need a resource contract
to be useful, which is the layers table's admission test for this tier.
The structure they render is a layout and lives one layer down —
`DetailPage` in `@marktiderman/genesis-ui/layout` — so an app with its own
fetching keeps the page shape without inheriting the provider. That
layout/data-bound pairing is the same one `AppShell` and `ResourcePage`
already have.

The three non-record states are rendered here rather than left to the
caller, because a per-app "loading…" is exactly the hand-written code a
template exists to remove:
- loading, or no id yet -> `PageLoading`
- absent -> `EmptyState` saying so, distinct from the error state, since a
  deleted record and a broken query need different words. Every provider
  Genesis ships signals "no such row" by throwing rather than by resolving
  empty, so this state is reached by classifying the error (see
  `isNotFoundError`) as well as by a falsy `data`
- any other failure -> `EmptyState` carrying the provider's message, which
  is kept verbatim: an error state that hides what went wrong is the one
  nobody can act on

`titleField` is exact: name a field and you get that field, empty string
included. The `name` -> `title` -> id chain is the DEFAULT, not a fallback
layered under an explicit choice — a page silently titled by a different
column than the one asked for is worse than a blank one.

props.name: children
props.description: The primary content region.

props.name: id
props.description:
Record id. Nullish means "not resolved yet" — no request goes out and the
page shows its loading state, which is what a route param that hasn't
arrived should look like. It is deliberately NOT the not-found state:

props.name: resource
props.description: Resource name, resolved through the mounted `DataProvider`.

props.name: actions
props.description: Record-scoped controls, built from the loaded record.

props.name: breadcrumb
props.description: Slot above the title: a `Breadcrumb`, a back link, a `StatusBadge`.

props.name: select
props.description: Provider select/join syntax, e.g. `"*, owner:profiles(name)"`.

props.name: sidebar
props.description: Metadata column, built from the loaded record.

props.name: subtitleField
props.description: Field used as the line under the title.

props.name: testID
props.description: Stable test/automation selector (emitted as `data-testid`).

props.name: titleField
props.description:
Field used as the page title. Defaults to `name`, then `title`, then the
id — the same fallback chain `ResourcePage` uses for a row's label.

props.name: autoPlaceholder
props.description:
Generate a placeholder ("Enter name") for fields whose `placeholder` is
unset. Default `false`: a placeholder that restates the label adds noise,
and reads as a filled value at a glance. A field's own `placeholder`
always shows. (Select fields keep their "Select…" prompt either way.)

props.name: columns
props.description: Number of columns for the form layout. Default 1.

props.name: layout
props.description: Layout mode for the form container. Default "dialog".

props.name: listData
props.description: Full dataset used to auto-detect select fields from unique values.

props.name: mode
props.description: Form presentation mode. Default "standard".

props.name: mutationMode
props.description:
When a save reaches the list. Default `"pessimistic"`: the form waits
for the provider. `"optimistic"` closes at once and updates the cached
list, putting it back (and toasting the error) if the save fails.
`"undoable"` does the same and shows an Undo toast; the save is sent
after `undoDelayMs` unless undone (or at once, undone by the provider,
when it serves `undo`). Needs a mounted `<Toaster />`.

props.name: onDirtyChange
props.description:
Called when the form becomes dirty or clean, with a `confirmLeave` that
asks when needed: the hook for a router blocker (SKILL.md "Unsaved
changes").

props.name: onUndoable
props.description: Replaces the undo toast.

props.name: prefillFromUrl
props.description:
Pre-fill a create form from the page URL: a query param named like a
field (`?status=draft`) becomes that field's starting value. Default
`true`, as before. Pass `false` when the page's query string means
something else — a list's own filters, say — and must not leak into the
new record.

props.name: steps
props.description: Wizard step definitions. Required when mode is "wizard".

props.name: undoDelayMs
props.description: How long an `undoable` save waits for an undo, in ms. Default 5000.

props.name: warnWhenUnsaved
props.description:
Warn before unsaved changes are lost. Default false. While the form is
dirty, Cancel / Esc / clicking outside asks first, and closing or
reloading the tab shows the browser's prompt. Pass `{ message }` to
change the question. For router navigation, see `onDirtyChange`.

components.name: ResourcePage
components.summary:
A list page for a resource: header, filters, table or cards, paging,
the open record's panel, and the built-in form and confirmed delete.
{@link useResourceTable } is the same behaviour without this markup.

props.name: allowCreate
props.description: Enable built-in create form (ignored if onCreate callback is provided).

props.name: allowDelete
props.description:
Built-in delete for `resource` mode (ignored if `onDelete` is
provided): the peek's Delete button opens a confirm dialog, then calls
`useResource`'s `remove` with the row's `getKey` (when supplied) or its
`id` — which invalidates the list — and closes the peek. A failure shows
in the dialog.

props.name: allowEdit
props.description: Enable built-in edit form (ignored if onEdit callback is provided).

props.name: bulkActions
props.type: { label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; variant?: "default" | "destructive"; onAction: (ids: string[]) => void | Promise<void>; disabled?: boolean | undefined; testId?: string | undefined; }[] | undefined

props.name: can
props.description:
What the signed-in user may do: `can("create")`, `can("edit", item)`,
`can("delete", item)`. Return false to hide the New button, or a row's
Edit or Delete (and the built-in edit form won't open for it). Omitted,
everything the handlers allow is offered. A UI gate only: the server
must still refuse the write.

props.name: canDelete
props.description:
@deprecated Use `can` — `can={(action, item) => action !== "delete" || !item || mayDelete(item)}`.
Still honoured: a row it refuses gets no Delete.

props.name: canEdit
props.description:
@deprecated Use `can` — `can={(action, item) => action !== "edit" || !item || mayEdit(item)}`.
Still honoured: a row it refuses gets no Edit.

props.name: canEditItem
canSaveViews
props.description: Show the "save current view" affordance.

props.name: capabilities
props.description:
What the data source can do. A control it can't serve is hidden rather
than left to error (DATA-STUDIO.md decision 9): `search: false` hides the
search box, `sort: false` the sort select. Pass a provider's
`capabilities()` straight in. Omitted, both show, as before.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the page shell's root.

props.name: clientRowLimit
props.description:
`pagination="client"` only: the most rows fetched. Default 1000. An
explicit `resourceOptions.defaultPerPage` wins. Keep it at or under the
provider's `maxPerPage` (`capabilities().maxPerPage`; 1000 by default for
Supabase): a larger page is refused, not cut short.

props.name: columnVisibility
props.description: Show the column-visibility dropdown. DataTable's default is `true`.

props.name: columnVisibilityKey
props.description: Persist key for the user's column-visibility picks.

props.name: confirmDelete
props.description:
Confirm before deleting. Defaults to `true` for `allowDelete` and
`false` for `onDelete` (which keeps its old, unconfirmed behaviour).
Pass an object to set the dialog's copy.

props.name: data
props.description: Server-data mode: pre-fetched data array.

props.name: defaultView
props.description:
The view shown until the user picks one with the view toggle. Default
`"table"`. Pass `{ mobile: "grid", desktop: "table" }` for cards on
phones and a table on desktops. Only an explicit pick is persisted, so
the responsive default stays responsive until the user chooses.

props.name: detail
props.description: How row-click detail is shown. Default "panel".

props.name: detailFields
props.type: { key: string; label: string; render?: ((value: unknown, item: T) => ReactNode); }[]

props.name: emptyDescription
props.description: A sentence under the empty-state title — forwarded to `DataPageShell`.

props.name: emptyIcon
props.description: The empty state's icon.

props.name: emptyMessage
props.description: The empty state's title, e.g. "No tasks yet". Default "No results found".

props.name: emptyState
props.description: The empty state's action, e.g. the create button.

props.name: error
props.description:
Server-data mode: the caller's fetch failed, so render the shell's error
panel instead of an empty table. Takes effect even when `data` is
non-empty — stale rows beside no indication of failure are exactly the
silent-failure this prop exists to prevent. Ignored in client-side mode,
where `useResource`'s own error state is used.

props.name: errorMessage
props.description:
Message shown in the error panel, in place of the shell's generic
"Failed to load …". Forwarded in both modes — it is inert unless an
error state is actually showing — so a client-side page can also give
its failure a human sentence.

props.name: filters
props.description:
Extra multi-select filter comboboxes, handed straight to `DataFilters`
and rendered beside the status chips. Each config owns its own
`selected` array and `onChange` — ResourcePage never reads or writes
them, because it cannot know what a caller's "Grade" or "Subject"
combobox means against the row shape. That is deliberate rather than a
gap: the built-in machinery (`searchFields`, `statusFilter`) covers the
two shapes it *can* interpret, and this prop covers everything else by
getting out of the way.

Two consequences of that hands-off stance, stated rather than hidden:
- These selections are invisible to `page.hasActiveFilters`, so the
  header's "Clear filters" affordance does not appear for them alone,
  and `onClearFilters` does not reset them. DataFilters' own "Clear all"
  does call each config's `onChange([])`, so wire real clearing there.
- In client-side mode the rows are NOT re-filtered by these selections.
  A caller using them is expected to filter its own `data` (or ask the
  server to), exactly as it already does in server-controlled mode.

props.name: formFields
props.description: Field definitions for the built-in form.

props.name: formLayout
props.description: Layout mode for the built-in form container. If not set, defaults to sheet for edit, dialog for create.

props.name: formMode
props.description: Form presentation mode. Default "standard".

props.name: formSteps
props.description: Wizard step definitions. Required when formMode is "wizard".

props.name: getKey
props.description:
A row's identity, for React keys and bulk selection. Defaults to
`String(item.id)`. Supply it for rows keyed some other way — a composite
key (`encodeRecordKey` from `@marktiderman/genesis-core/schema`), or a
table whose key column isn't called `id`. Detail `route` mode still
navigates by `item.id`.

props.name: getSubtitle
props.description:
The detail peek's subtitle, computed from the row ("2 staff", "Due
Friday"). Wins over `subtitleField`, which can only show one column
verbatim.

props.name: getTitle
props.description:
Name a record from more than one field (`${first} ${last}`). Wins over
`titleField` for the detail title and the card's accessible name.

props.name: gridCols
props.description:
Tailwind grid-column classes for the card grid, passed through to
`DataGrid`'s `gridCols` — e.g. `"grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3"`.
Defaults to DataGrid's own responsive 1/2/3/4-column ramp.

props.name: header
props.description:
`"page"` (default) renders the full header with the title. `"toolbar"`
keeps the header's actions (count, view toggle, settings, create) and
drops the title block — for a list inside a tab or card whose page
already has the heading. See `DataPageShell`'s `header`.

props.name: keyboardNavigation
props.description:
Built-in list keyboard navigation via `useKeyboardNavigation`: j/k (or
Arrow Up/Down) move a focus cursor, Enter opens the focused item,
Backspace (⌫) closes an open detail view, and x toggles the focused
item's selection when `bulkActions` are configured. Set to `false` to
opt out.

Default-on, and scoped so that being on by default stays safe:
- The j/k cursor runs while the grid or list view is showing. Table view
  keeps its own sort/pagination, so there `DataTable` handles the keys on
  its focusable rows instead (↑/↓ or j/k, Home/End, Enter, x); this prop
  turns that off too.
- Cursor keys suspend while a detail panel/modal or the built-in form
  is open, so they can't drive the list behind the overlay; ⌫ stays
  live there so it can close it.
- Backspace is only intercepted while there's an open detail to close.
- Modified chords (Ctrl/Cmd/Alt) are never captured, so an app's
  Cmd+K-style shortcuts keep working.

props.name: live
props.description:
`resource` mode: refetch the list (and the open record) when the
provider reports a change, e.g. Supabase Realtime. Shorthand for
`resourceOptions.live`, which wins. See core's `UseResourceOptions.live`.

props.name: loading
props.description:
Server-data mode: the caller's fetch is in flight, so render the shell's
loading skeleton instead of the (as yet meaningless) `data`. Ignored in
client-side mode, where `useResource`'s own loading state is used.

props.name: mutationMode
props.description:
When the built-in form's saves and deletes reach the list: `"pessimistic"`
(default, wait for the provider), `"optimistic"` or `"undoable"` (an Undo
toast). See ResourceForm `mutationMode`. `resourceOptions.mutationMode`
wins for deletes.

props.name: onDelete
props.description:
Delete handler, shown as the detail peek's Delete button. Called
directly, as before, unless `confirmDelete` is set — then it runs after
the confirm dialog, which shows its error if the returned promise
rejects, and closes the peek when it resolves.

props.name: onDeleted
props.description: Called after a confirmed or built-in delete succeeds — e.g. a toast.

props.name: onNavigate
props.description:
Imperative navigation used only when `detail="route"` (navigates to
`/{resource}/{id}` on row click). Defaults to a full-page navigation.
Router consumers pass their navigate fn — e.g. RR `useNavigate()` or
Next `router.push`.

props.name: onPageChange
props.description:
Called with the next 1-based page number. The pager only renders when
this is supplied AND both `perPage` and `total` are supplied — see
{@link perPage} and {@link total}. Supplying this without either one
renders an error naming the missing props instead of a pager.

Status changes reach the server through `onFiltersChange` — not a
dedicated callback here — because `statusFilter` state is tracked by
the same filter machinery that already calls `onFiltersChange`
regardless of controlled mode (see {@link statusFilter}). In
server-controlled mode a status change also calls `onPageChange(1)`
directly, since the previous page number is meaningless against a new
filtered result set.

props.name: onPerPageChange

props.name: pagination
props.description:

`data` (server-data mode pages through the controlled props instead).

  and search, sort, filter and page them in the browser — header-click
  sort and instant search keep working. If the resource holds more rows
  than that, a notice under the list says how many are shown (and a
  console warning names this prop), rather than silently truncating.
- `"server"`: fetch one page at a time. The pager under the list drives
  `useResource`'s page, the header's page size its `perPage`, and
  search / sort / status chips become provider queries (search is
  debounced), and the current page stays on screen while the next one
  loads. Give `statusFilter` explicit `options` here — derived ones can
  only see the current page's values. Search needs `searchFields` (or
  `resourceOptions.searchFields`) — the provider must be told which
  columns to match — so the search box is hidden without them. Table
  header sorting is withdrawn, as in server-data mode; the sort control
  in the filter row drives the query.

  else the stored page size) and a "Load more" button appends the next
  page, by cursor where the provider serves it
  (`capabilities().cursorPagination`) and by offset otherwise. The
  server orders by `resourceOptions.defaultSort`; search, sort and
  filters in the toolbar act on the rows loaded so far.

cannot be inferred from `data.length`, because a short final page is
smaller than the real page size. Wins over the per-user page size
persisted by `viewSettingsKey` — an explicit prop always beats a stored
preference.

Required whenever `onPageChange` is supplied. A short final page (the
server's last page returning fewer rows than its page size) is
indistinguishable from a small page size — there is no correct way to
infer the divisor from the rows handed back. Rather than guess and
render a wrong range or a stuck Next button, the component refuses to
render the pager and shows an error instead when `onPageChange` is
present without `perPage`.

names every missing prop, not just the first.

renderer there). ResourcePage still owns data-fetching, filtering,
sorting, and layout (grid columns, infinite-scroll batching, stagger
animation) — this only swaps what's rendered inside each item slot.

plus `open()` to activate the row (opening the configured detail
panel/modal/route). Row activation is *not* applied automatically to a
custom card — wrapping it would double-fire against cards that bring
their own click handling and would hijack clicks on nested buttons — so
call `actions.open()` from wherever your card should activate.

click-through, selection, density, column visibility and resizing are

wire for itself. That is the trade this prop makes, and it is why
`renderCard` remains the lighter option when only the *cells* need to
change — a `ResourceColumnDef.render` is lighter still.

primitives.summary:
ScrollArea — a scroll container with a consistent, styled scrollbar.

Backed by Radix `ScrollArea`. The hand-rolled version was a single
`overflow-auto` div plus a stack of `::-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-element
rules, which is a WebKit-only vocabulary: Firefox ignored every one of them
and rendered the OS scrollbar instead, so the "design system scrollbar" was
a Chrome/Safari-only promise. Radix hides the native scrollbar and renders a
real element in its place, so the same thumb appears in every browser, can
be dragged, and participates in the same hover/transition styling as the
rest of the system.

`type` defaults to `"auto"` — scrollbar present exactly while the content
overflows — because that is what `overflow-auto` did. Radix's own default is
`"hover"`; pass `type` explicitly for `"hover"`, `"always"` or `"scroll"`.

NOTE ON PROP DESTINATIONS. This used to be one element; it is now a root plus
an inner viewport, and the root does not scroll. Three props therefore have to
be routed inward rather than spread onto the root with the rest, because for
them the root is not merely a different element — it is an element on which
they do nothing at all, silently:

  - `onScroll` / `onScrollCapture` — `scroll` events do not bubble, so a
    handler on the root would never fire once. Infinite-loading and
    scroll-position UI would break with no error.
  - `nonce` — Radix injects its scrollbar-hiding `<style>` from the viewport
    and only reads a nonce given to that component. Under a strict
    `style-src 'nonce-…'` policy the rule is blocked and the native scrollbar
    shows up alongside the custom one.

Everything else keeps landing on the root, which is the component's box and
the right owner for `className`, `style`, `id`, `role`, `aria-*`, `data-*`
and bubbling handlers. `viewportProps` is the escape hatch for the remainder
— most importantly a `ref`, since `ref` on this component addresses the root
and setting `scrollTop` there does nothing.

SettingsPage — a sectioned settings surface with a nav rail for jumping
between sections.

```tsx
<SettingsPage
  title="Workspace settings"
  sections={[
    {
      id: "profile",
      title: "Profile",
      content: <SettingsRow label="Display name" htmlFor="name"><Input id="name" /></SettingsRow>,
    },
    {
      id: "notifications",
      title: "Notifications",
      description: "How and when we contact you.",
      content: <ToggleRow label="Weekly digest" checked={digest} onCheckedChange={setDigest} />,
    },
  ]}
/>
```

titles and ids. Declaring each once is what makes "the rail says
Notifications and the heading says Alerts" unrepresentable.

with a single entry is a link to where you already are. That is an
automatic consequence of the content rather than a prop, so nobody has to
remember to turn it off.

in both modes rather than an oversight: side by side it is a stretched
grid item, so it sticks for the length of the sections; stacked, its pane
is exactly its own height, so sticky positioning has nothing to travel
and it simply scrolls away. One class, right twice.

landmark a screen-reader user can jump to, which is the whole promise the
visual rail is making.

`PageHeader` — see `./detail-page` for the measured reasons composing it
was rejected across all four templates. Width is left to `Container` —
wrap, don't duplicate.

setting is stored, and when, is the app's. Genesis's answer for the
storing half is `useStorage` from `@marktiderman/genesis-core`, which a
caller wires up outside this component.

primitives.summary:
A spreadsheet grid: virtualized rows, a keyboard-driven active cell and
range, in-place editing, and copy and paste through the system clipboard
as tab-separated text, so it round-trips with Sheets and Excel.

Keys: arrows, Tab and Shift+Tab move; Shift+arrows extend the range;
Enter or F2 edits (Enter again saves and moves down); typing starts an
edit; Escape cancels; Delete clears; Home/End and Ctrl+Home/End jump;
PageUp/PageDown move a screen; Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes.

Why it isn't Radix (docs/FRAMEWORK.md rule 3): Radix has no data grid.
The focus model follows the WAI-ARIA grid pattern instead: one tab stop
(the grid), the active cell exposed through aria-activedescendant, and
aria-selected for the range, so a screen reader announces each move.
Virtualization comes from TanStack Virtual (decision 20's spike: stable,
headless, actively released; react-data-grid's latest has been a beta for
years and brings its own CSS).

primitives.summary:
Tabs — a tablist and its panels.

Backed by Radix `Tabs`. The hand-rolled version was a React context plus a
row of plain `<button>`s: it tracked the selected value correctly and
nothing else. Every keyboard and screen-reader affordance the WAI-ARIA tabs
pattern asks for was missing — `role="tablist"`/`"tab"`/`"tabpanel"`, the
`aria-selected` state, the `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` link between a
tab and its panel, the roving `tabindex` that makes the whole tablist ONE
tab stop instead of N, and Arrow/Home/End navigation between tabs. Radix
supplies all of it, plus the selection state the old version already
handled.

One behavioural note worth knowing: Radix selects on `mousedown` rather than
`click`. Pointer users see no difference, but a synthetic `fireEvent.click`
on a trigger no longer changes tabs.

primitives.summary:
Toolbar — a grouped set of controls that behaves as ONE tab stop.

This is a primitive, not a layout, and the distinction is the whole reason
it wraps Radix instead of a `<div className="flex gap-1">`. Radix's Toolbar
owns a roving tabindex: Tab moves into and out of the whole group, and
Arrow/Home/End move between the items inside it. A layout, by the framework's
own definition, "positions things without knowing what they are" — this one
knows its children are focusable controls and manages their focus, so it
fails that test and passes the primitive one.

`orientation` is passed to BOTH Radix (which uses it to decide whether
Left/Right or Up/Down are the navigation keys) and the CVA class (which uses
it to decide the flex direction). Splitting those would let the visual axis
and the keyboard axis disagree — arrows moving "down" a row of buttons.

props.name: testID

props.name: testID

primitives.summary:
Tooltip — hover/focus hint anchored to its trigger child. Backed by Radix `Tooltip`, which owns the parts a design system should not be maintaining itself: open/close state, the pointer delay, opening on keyboard focus and closing on blur/Escape/scroll, the portal, collision detection against the viewport, and the `aria-describedby` ↔ `role="tooltip"` association. The previous implementation was CSS-only — a `group` wrapper plus `group-hover:block` / `group-focus-within:block` — which meant no portal (so the bubble was clipped by any `overflow:hidden` ancestor), no collision handling (so it ran off-screen at the edges), no dismissal, and no delay. The wrapper `
` stays, and keeps `group relative inline-flex`: it is where `className` and the rest of `HTMLAttributes` land, so removing it would silently drop props callers already pass. Positioning no longer depends on it. The bubble keeps `whitespace-nowrap`, so rich `content` does not soft wrap by itself — long multi-line content needs an explicit `
`, or a `whitespace-normal` + width class on the node you pass in. Dropping `whitespace-nowrap` here would re-wrap every existing single-line string tooltip, so it stays opt-out rather than opt-in.

props.name: content
props.description:
Tooltip body. Accepts any `ReactNode` — icons, formatted or multi-line

props.name: delayDuration
props.description:

opens. Keyboard focus is never delayed — Radix opens instantly on focus
regardless of this value.

Defaults to `0` rather than Radix's own `700`: the CSS-only

components.summary:
The undo toast for an `undoable` write (core's `onUndoable`): a sonner

props.name: commit
props.description: Send a `delay` write now.

props.name: delayMs

props.name: strategy

- `provider`: the write was sent at once, because the provider serves

props.name: undo

sent), false when it could not be: already sent under `delay` (the
window closed, it was committed, a later write on the same record sent
it first, or the page unloaded), already undone, or the provider's undo
failed (reported through `onError`). Works after the hook that made the
write has unmounted. Safe to call more than once.

props.name: id

primitives.summary:
The list behind {@link ResourcePage }, without any markup: where the rows
come from (a `resource` through the data provider, or `data` you pass),
search, sort, status filter and paging, selection, the open record (and
its URL state), the built-in create/edit form and confirmed delete, and
the row handlers. Takes the same options as `ResourcePage`.

Use it to build a different layout over the same behaviour; `ResourcePage`
itself is this behaviour plus Genesis's markup.

components.name: useResourceTableModel
components.summary:
Everything ResourcePage's markup reads. Internal: its names may change in
any release. Apps use {@link useResourceTable}.

props.name: allowCreate
props.description: Enable built-in create form (ignored if onCreate callback is provided).

props.name: allowDelete
props.description:
Built-in delete for `resource` mode (ignored if `onDelete` is
provided): the peek's Delete button opens a confirm dialog, then calls
`useResource`'s `remove` with the row's `getKey` (when supplied) or its
`id` — which invalidates the list — and closes the peek. A failure shows
in the dialog.

props.name: allowEdit
props.description: Enable built-in edit form (ignored if onEdit callback is provided).

props.name: bulkActions
props.type: { label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; variant?: "default" | "destructive"; onAction: (ids: string[]) => void | Promise<void>; disabled?: boolean | undefined; testId?: string | undefined; }[] | undefined

props.name: can
props.description:
What the signed-in user may do: `can("create")`, `can("edit", item)`,
`can("delete", item)`. Return false to hide the New button, or a row's
Edit or Delete (and the built-in edit form won't open for it). Omitted,
everything the handlers allow is offered. A UI gate only: the server
must still refuse the write.

props.name: canDelete
props.description:
@deprecated Use `can` — `can={(action, item) => action !== "delete" || !item || mayDelete(item)}`.
Still honoured: a row it refuses gets no Delete.

props.name: canEdit
props.description:
@deprecated Use `can` — `can={(action, item) => action !== "edit" || !item || mayEdit(item)}`.
Still honoured: a row it refuses gets no Edit.

props.name: canEditItem
canSaveViews
props.description: Show the "save current view" affordance.

props.name: capabilities
props.description:
What the data source can do. A control it can't serve is hidden rather
than left to error (DATA-STUDIO.md decision 9): `search: false` hides the
search box, `sort: false` the sort select. Pass a provider's
`capabilities()` straight in. Omitted, both show, as before.

props.name: className
props.description: Merged onto the page shell's root.

props.name: clientRowLimit
props.description:
`pagination="client"` only: the most rows fetched. Default 1000. An
explicit `resourceOptions.defaultPerPage` wins. Keep it at or under the
provider's `maxPerPage` (`capabilities().maxPerPage`; 1000 by default for
Supabase): a larger page is refused, not cut short.

props.name: columnVisibility
props.description: Show the column-visibility dropdown. DataTable's default is `true`.

props.name: columnVisibilityKey
props.description: Persist key for the user's column-visibility picks.

props.name: confirmDelete
props.description:
Confirm before deleting. Defaults to `true` for `allowDelete` and
`false` for `onDelete` (which keeps its old, unconfirmed behaviour).
Pass an object to set the dialog's copy.

props.name: data
props.description: Server-data mode: pre-fetched data array.

props.name: defaultView
props.description:
The view shown until the user picks one with the view toggle. Default
`"table"`. Pass `{ mobile: "grid", desktop: "table" }` for cards on
phones and a table on desktops. Only an explicit pick is persisted, so
the responsive default stays responsive until the user chooses.

props.name: detail
props.description: How row-click detail is shown. Default "panel".

props.name: detailFields
props.type: { key: string; label: string; render?: ((value: unknown, item: T) => ReactNode); }[]

props.name: emptyDescription
props.description: A sentence under the empty-state title — forwarded to `DataPageShell`.

props.name: emptyIcon
props.description: The empty state's icon.

props.name: emptyMessage
props.description: The empty state's title, e.g. "No tasks yet". Default "No results found".

props.name: emptyState
props.description: The empty state's action, e.g. the create button.

props.name: error
props.description:
Server-data mode: the caller's fetch failed, so render the shell's error
panel instead of an empty table. Takes effect even when `data` is
non-empty — stale rows beside no indication of failure are exactly the
silent-failure this prop exists to prevent. Ignored in client-side mode,
where `useResource`'s own error state is used.

props.name: errorMessage
props.description:
Message shown in the error panel, in place of the shell's generic
"Failed to load …". Forwarded in both modes — it is inert unless an
error state is actually showing — so a client-side page can also give
its failure a human sentence.

props.name: filters
props.description:
Extra multi-select filter comboboxes, handed straight to `DataFilters`
and rendered beside the status chips. Each config owns its own
`selected` array and `onChange` — ResourcePage never reads or writes
them, because it cannot know what a caller's "Grade" or "Subject"
combobox means against the row shape. That is deliberate rather than a
gap: the built-in machinery (`searchFields`, `statusFilter`) covers the
two shapes it *can* interpret, and this prop covers everything else by
getting out of the way.

Two consequences of that hands-off stance, stated rather than hidden:
- These selections are invisible to `page.hasActiveFilters`, so the
  header's "Clear filters" affordance does not appear for them alone,
  and `onClearFilters` does not reset them. DataFilters' own "Clear all"
  does call each config's `onChange([])`, so wire real clearing there.
- In client-side mode the rows are NOT re-filtered by these selections.
  A caller using them is expected to filter its own `data` (or ask the
  server to), exactly as it already does in server-controlled mode.

props.name: formFields
props.description: Field definitions for the built-in form.

props.name: formLayout
props.description: Layout mode for the built-in form container. If not set, defaults to sheet for edit, dialog for create.

props.name: formMode
props.description: Form presentation mode. Default "standard".

props.name: formSteps
props.description: Wizard step definitions. Required when formMode is "wizard".

props.name: getKey
props.description:
A row's identity, for React keys and bulk selection. Defaults to
`String(item.id)`. Supply it for rows keyed some other way — a composite
key (`encodeRecordKey` from `@marktiderman/genesis-core/schema`), or a
table whose key column isn't called `id`. Detail `route` mode still
navigates by `item.id`.

props.name: getSubtitle
props.description:
The detail peek's subtitle, computed from the row ("2 staff", "Due
Friday"). Wins over `subtitleField`, which can only show one column
verbatim.

props.name: getTitle
props.description:
Name a record from more than one field (`${first} ${last}`). Wins over
`titleField` for the detail title and the card's accessible name.

props.name: gridCols
props.description:
Tailwind grid-column classes for the card grid, passed through to
`DataGrid`'s `gridCols` — e.g. `"grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3"`.
Defaults to DataGrid's own responsive 1/2/3/4-column ramp.

props.name: header
props.description:
`"page"` (default) renders the full header with the title. `"toolbar"`
keeps the header's actions (count, view toggle, settings, create) and
drops the title block — for a list inside a tab or card whose page
already has the heading. See `DataPageShell`'s `header`.

props.name: keyboardNavigation
props.description:
Built-in list keyboard navigation via `useKeyboardNavigation`: j/k (or
Arrow Up/Down) move a focus cursor, Enter opens the focused item,
Backspace (⌫) closes an open detail view, and x toggles the focused
item's selection when `bulkActions` are configured. Set to `false` to
opt out.

Default-on, and scoped so that being on by default stays safe:
- The j/k cursor runs while the grid or list view is showing. Table view
  keeps its own sort/pagination, so there `DataTable` handles the keys on
  its focusable rows instead (↑/↓ or j/k, Home/End, Enter, x); this prop
  turns that off too.
- Cursor keys suspend while a detail panel/modal or the built-in form
  is open, so they can't drive the list behind the overlay; ⌫ stays
  live there so it can close it.
- Backspace is only intercepted while there's an open detail to close.
- Modified chords (Ctrl/Cmd/Alt) are never captured, so an app's
  Cmd+K-style shortcuts keep working.

props.name: live
props.description:
`resource` mode: refetch the list (and the open record) when the
provider reports a change, e.g. Supabase Realtime. Shorthand for
`resourceOptions.live`, which wins. See core's `UseResourceOptions.live`.

props.name: loading
props.description:
Server-data mode: the caller's fetch is in flight, so render the shell's
loading skeleton instead of the (as yet meaningless) `data`. Ignored in
client-side mode, where `useResource`'s own loading state is used.

props.name: mutationMode
props.description:
When the built-in form's saves and deletes reach the list: `"pessimistic"`
(default, wait for the provider), `"optimistic"` or `"undoable"` (an Undo
toast). See ResourceForm `mutationMode`. `resourceOptions.mutationMode`
wins for deletes.

props.name: onDelete
props.description:
Delete handler, shown as the detail peek's Delete button. Called
directly, as before, unless `confirmDelete` is set — then it runs after
the confirm dialog, which shows its error if the returned promise
rejects, and closes the peek when it resolves.

props.name: onDeleted
props.description: Called after a confirmed or built-in delete succeeds — e.g. a toast.

props.name: onNavigate
props.description:
Imperative navigation used only when `detail="route"` (navigates to
`/{resource}/{id}` on row click). Defaults to a full-page navigation.
Router consumers pass their navigate fn — e.g. RR `useNavigate()` or
Next `router.push`.

props.name: onPageChange
props.description:
Called with the next 1-based page number. The pager only renders when
this is supplied AND both `perPage` and `total` are supplied — see
{@link perPage} and {@link total}. Supplying this without either one
renders an error naming the missing props instead of a pager.

Status changes reach the server through `onFiltersChange` — not a
dedicated callback here — because `statusFilter` state is tracked by
the same filter machinery that already calls `onFiltersChange`
regardless of controlled mode (see {@link statusFilter}). In
server-controlled mode a status change also calls `onPageChange(1)`
directly, since the previous page number is meaningless against a new
filtered result set.

props.name: onPerPageChange
props.description: Called when the user picks a different page size in the header's view settings.

props.name: onRetry
props.description:
Server-data mode: invoked by the error panel's Retry button. The button
only appears when this is supplied, so a caller with no way to retry
simply omits it and gets an error panel without a dead control. In
client-side mode the button is already wired to `useResource`'s own
`refetch` and this prop is ignored.

props.name: onSearchChange
props.description: Called when the user changes the search text (including clearing it).

props.name: onSortChange
props.description: Called when the user changes the sort, with `null` when the sort is cleared.

props.name: openOnCardClick
props.description:
With a custom `renderCard`: make each whole card (and list row) one
keyboard-reachable button that opens the detail, so the card needs no
`actions.open()` wiring and no hand-rolled `div role="button"`. Links and
buttons inside the card keep their own clicks. Off by default, because
an existing card that already calls `open()` would fire it twice.

props.name: page
props.description: Current page, 1-based. Server-controlled mode only.

props.name: pageSizeOptions
props.description:
Page-size choices offered by `DataTable`'s own pager. Client-side mode
only — server-controlled mode switches that pager off. (The header's
view-settings popover has its own fixed 10/25/50/100 list.)

props.name: pagination
props.description:
How `resource` mode reaches rows past the first page. Ignored with
`data` (server-data mode pages through the controlled props instead).

- `"client"` (default): fetch up to `clientRowLimit` rows in one request
  and search, sort, filter and page them in the browser — header-click
  sort and instant search keep working. If the resource holds more rows
  than that, a notice under the list says how many are shown (and a
  console warning names this prop), rather than silently truncating.
- `"server"`: fetch one page at a time. The pager under the list drives
  `useResource`'s page, the header's page size its `perPage`, and
  search / sort / status chips become provider queries (search is
  debounced), and the current page stays on screen while the next one
  loads. Give `statusFilter` explicit `options` here — derived ones can
  only see the current page's values. Search needs `searchFields` (or
  `resourceOptions.searchFields`) — the provider must be told which

props.description:

panel instead of an empty table. Takes effect even when `data` is
non-empty — stale rows beside no indication of failure are exactly the

where `useResource`'s own error state is used.

error state is actually showing — so a client-side page can also give

UserAvatar — canonical user-identity avatar. Shows the person's photo when
`src` is set and loads successfully; otherwise (including a failed image
load — Radix's Avatar swaps to the fallback automatically) it falls back
to initials computed from `name`. Wraps the lower-level
`Avatar`/`AvatarImage`/`AvatarFallback` primitives so call sites stop
hand-rolling initials logic per-usage.

The root carries `role="img"` + `aria-label={name}` so the person's full name
is the accessible name on BOTH paths — without it the fallback route renders
a bare `span`, a generic element whose author-supplied label AT may ignore,
announcing only the visible initials ("AL").

primitives.summary:
VisuallyHidden — content removed from the visual layout but kept in the
accessibility tree.

This is the correct tool for the label an icon-only control needs, for the
`DialogTitle` a dialog must have even when the design shows none, and for
live-region status text. It is NOT `display: none` and it is NOT
`visibility: hidden` — both of those remove the node from the a11y tree too,
which is the exact opposite of the intent.

Why Radix rather than Tailwind's `sr-only`: the two produce the same result,
but `sr-only` is a class a consumer's `@apply`, a purge misconfiguration, or
a competing utility can quietly defeat, and the failure is silent — the text
simply becomes visible, or the layout shifts, and nothing in a build catches
it. Radix applies the clip rectangle as inline styles on the element itself,
so there is no stylesheet for the consumer's build to lose.

**That robustness cuts both ways, and it is the one thing to know before
reaching for this.** An inline style beats any ordinary class declaration, so
a `className` cannot override the clipping either — not accidentally, and
